name: Andrew Wiggins
notes: Kansas freshman billed as the top prospect since Kevin Durant, an elite-tier athlete already playing plus defense (17.1/5.9/1.5) but with statistics that hedged against instant superstardom — evaluators noted he was better than his box score because of his defensive potential, not because he'd dominated the ball at Kansas. Cleveland took him 1st. The career never became the offensive star some hoped for, but after a 2020 trade to Golden State, Wiggins found the ideal role — a plus wing defender and secondary scorer who started for the 2022 championship team (18.3/8.8 in that Finals) before being dealt to Miami in 2025. Mixed outcome: a genuine title-winning starter and one-time All-Star, but never the No.1-pick-caliber offensive engine the selection implied.

name: Jabari Parker
notes: Duke's most complete offensive freshman in the class (19.1/8.7), a pro-ready jumpshot and post game that had him in the 1-vs-1 conversation with Wiggins, with defense and conditioning flagged as the real questions. Milwaukee took him 2nd. The Bucks got a legitimate scorer in flashes (15.3/5.5 across four seasons) but two separate ACL tears on the same knee — the first ending his rookie year, the second wiping out most of year three — sapped the athleticism the whole profile depended on, and he never became more than a streaky scorer after leaving Milwaukee in 2018. Bust: a true top-2-pick talent derailed almost entirely by the exact knee, hit twice.

name: Joel Embiid
notes: Kansas center compared early to Hakeem Olajuwon for his back-to-the-basket footwork and two-way tools (11.2/8.1/2.6 blk before a season-ending back injury), but explicitly flagged as the least NBA-ready of the top prospects — low IQ moments, foul trouble, and now real injury-risk questions layered on top of the physical upside. Philadelphia took him 3rd anyway and waited two full seasons for his NBA debut. What followed is one of the great boom-outcomes of the class: a 2023 MVP (33.1/10.2/4.2/1.7) and perennial top-5 player, capped by exactly the durability question flagged pre-draft — Embiid has missed roughly as many regular-season games as he's played across his career. Hit, unambiguously, despite the games missed.

name: Aaron Gordon
notes: Arizona freshman billed pre-draft as the best defender in the class — explosive, fundamentally sound, versatile — with one glaring hole: he couldn't shoot, hitting only 42.1% from the line as a freshman. Orlando took him 4th. Gordon became exactly that: an elite play-finishing, switch-everything athlete who never developed a reliable jumper, but found his ceiling after a 2021 trade to Denver, where he became Nikola Jokić's ideal frontcourt partner and a starter on the 2023 championship team — also building a legendary (if title-less) dunk contest résumé along the way. Solid outcome: a genuine winning-team difference-maker who became exactly the plus-defense, shaky-jumper player scouted, just in a much bigger role than expected.

name: Danté Exum
notes: An 18-year-old Australian with almost no evaluable sample — hype built on two international tournaments — but real size-and-speed appeal for a combo guard (6'6" with a 6'9" wingspan), with decision-making and perimeter shooting flagged as unproven. Utah took him 5th on pure upside. The unproven-sample risk played out as injuries rather than skill failure: a torn ACL in 2015 started a chain of shoulder and kneecap issues that limited him to a bit-part, injury-interrupted career across Utah, Cleveland and Dallas (career 6.2/2.3), with his best stretch (7.8/2.9 in 2023-24) coming a decade after the pick. Bust relative to a top-5 selection — the talent flashed, but availability never did.

name: Marcus Smart
notes: Oklahoma State sophomore already regarded as the best on-ball defender in the class — a bulldog, multi-position stopper (3.5 steals per 40) with a shaky jumper (29.9% from three) as the one real question mark. Boston took him 6th. Smart became precisely that vision realized at the highest level: nine seasons anchoring Boston's defense through five Conference Finals and a 2022 Finals run, capped by the 2021-22 Defensive Player of the Year award — the first guard to win it since Gary Payton. Hit: the shooting limitation never fully resolved, but the two-way winning value scouted at Oklahoma State showed up exactly as projected, injuries later shortening stops in Memphis and Washington before a move to the Lakers.

name: Julius Randle
notes: Kentucky's bruising, do-it-all freshman four (15.0/10.4, 24 double-doubles) who helped lead the Wildcats to the title game — an ideal-frame power forward with All-Star upside contingent on the jumper coming along, per Zach Randolph comps. Los Angeles took him 7th, and a broken leg in his very first regular-season game delayed the payoff. It arrived eventually and then some: after stops with the Lakers and Pelicans, Randle became a 3x All-Star and 2021 Most Improved Player with the Knicks, developing exactly the perimeter shooting scouts had flagged as the swing skill. Hit: the All-Star-caliber offensive engine scouted at Kentucky, just on a longer timeline.

name: Nik Stauskas
notes: Michigan's Big Ten Player of the Year off a two-year, 44%-plus three-point barrage — pure shooting was the whole case, with average speed, leaping and lateral quickness the honest concerns, and a Kevin Martin one-way comp attached. Sacramento took him 8th. The one-way profile held: Stauskas bounced through six teams over eight seasons (Kings, 76ers, Nets, Trail Blazers, Cavaliers, Heat) as a streaky specialist, never developing into more than a low-minutes shooting reserve (6.7/2.0/1.5 career). Bust relative to a top-10 selection — the shooting translated only partially, and nothing else did.

name: Noah Vonleh
notes: Indiana's Big Ten Freshman of the Year and rebounding leader (11.3/9.0/1.4 blk), an inside-out four who could score on the block, protect the rim and hit an occasional three (16-of-33) — comps ran from Chris Bosh to Derrick Favors, real star-level upside if the skills matured together. Charlotte took him 9th. They never fully came together: Vonleh bounced through eight teams in a nomadic career, never developing into more than fringe frontcourt depth despite legitimate physical tools. Bust: the tantalizing all-around freshman flash at Indiana never translated into a real, lasting NBA role.

name: Elfrid Payton
notes: A late-blooming Louisiana-Lafayette junior (19.2/6.0/5.9) who shot up boards on elite length (6'7" wingspan) and playmaking vision at the point guard spot, with an obvious, glaring hole: almost no perimeter jumper and turnover-prone decision-making. Philadelphia took him 10th and immediately dealt him to Orlando for Dario Šarić's rights. Payton's career matched that profile closely — a long, well-traveled run (Magic, Suns, Pelicans, Knicks and more) as a defense-and-playmaking lead guard who never solved the outside shot that was flagged from day one. Mixed outcome: a real, decade-plus NBA starter/rotation guard, permanently capped by the exact shooting hole scouts identified.

name: Doug McDermott
notes: College basketball's all-time leading scorer (3,150 points at Creighton), a supremely polished, multi-level shot-maker who projected as, at worst, an elite spot-up threat — the flagged concern was a lack of athleticism and a tweener frame that made him a defensive liability at both forward spots. Denver took him 11th (traded to Chicago). McDermott became exactly the shooting specialist projected: a long, useful career (Bulls, Thunder, Pacers, Spurs, Kings and more) as a movement shooter and instant offense off the bench, never solving the defensive limitations flagged pre-draft. Mixed outcome: a real decade-plus NBA role built on the one elite skill scouted, capped everywhere else exactly as predicted.

name: Dario Šarić
notes: A 20-year-old Croatian point-forward with rare feel and passing vision for his size (6'10") and a legitimate stretch shot, but limited athleticism that made his NBA timeline uncertain. Orlando took him 12th and immediately dealt him to Philadelphia for Elfrid Payton's rights; Šarić spent two extra years developing in Turkey before his 2016 debut. He became precisely the skilled, high-IQ stretch four scouted — a long, valuable rotation career (76ers, Timberwolves, Suns, Thunder, Warriors, Nuggets, Kings) as a smart passer and floor-spacer, never an All-Star but a winning-team contributor everywhere he landed. Mixed outcome: real, lasting value, just short of the star billing his skill set once implied.

name: Zach LaVine
notes: UCLA's rawest lottery-caliber prospect — a bench player as a freshman (9.4/2.5) whose entire case was elite tools: a 41.5" combine vertical, real shooting touch (37.5% from three), and top-tier foot speed, with almost no proven feel, defensive IQ, or effort level to point to. Minnesota took him 13th on pure ceiling. LaVine became one of the class's biggest developmental hits: a 2x Slam Dunk champion who grew into a legitimate go-to scorer and 2x All-Star, most notably during a long, high-usage run with Chicago. Hit: the athletic tools scouts bet on translated into a genuine, sustained NBA offensive engine.

name: T.J. Warren
notes: NC State's ACC Player of the Year and scoring champion (24.9 ppg), a Caron Butler-comp bucket-getter with a smooth midrange package — but scouts flagged him as fairly one-dimensional, no real defense, playmaking, or rebounding to speak of. Phoenix took him 14th. Warren lived up to the pure-scorer profile in flashes, most memorably an explosive 2020 NBA-bubble stretch with Indiana (31.0 ppg, including a 53-point game), but chronic foot injuries derailed the back half of his career across stops with the Pacers, Nets and Suns. Mixed outcome: a legitimately elite scoring talent when healthy, undone by durability rather than skill.

name: Adreian Payne
notes: Michigan State's late-blooming senior stretch four (16.4/7.4 on 43.2% from three, capped by a 41-point NCAA Tournament outing), with prototypical inside-out size (7'4" wingspan) but real concern about a narrow lower body handling an 82-game NBA workload. Atlanta took him 15th (traded to Minnesota). The durability concern proved decisive — Payne never carved out a real NBA rotation role across stops with the Hawks, Timberwolves, Magic and Wolves again, playing sparingly before his NBA career ended by his mid-20s. Bust: the physical-durability question flagged pre-draft is exactly what kept a skilled stretch big off the floor.

name: Jusuf Nurkić
notes: A largely unscouted Bosnian center (no combine, no individual workouts) dominating Adriatic League competition — big, mobile, and producing at a 33/14/4.1 steal-and-block per-40 rate that hinted at a rare blend of size and agility. Denver took him 16th. Nurkić validated that upside emphatically after a 2017 trade to Portland, becoming a legitimate starting center — an All-Rookie honoree who anchored Portland's frontcourt for years (including a 2017-18 stretch run many credited as saving the Blazers' season) before injuries and later moves to Phoenix and Charlotte. Solid outcome: a real, long-term starting NBA center, exactly the two-way anchor the sparse pre-draft tape suggested.

name: James Young
notes: Kentucky's one-and-done sharpshooter off a title-game run (37 points combined in the Wildcats' final two tournament games), a pretty outside stroke paired with explicitly poor defense and shot creation. Boston took him 17th. The defensive and shot-creation gaps never closed — Young settled into a brief NBA run (Celtics, 76ers) before falling out of the league in his mid-20s and continuing his career overseas. Bust: the outside shot flashed exactly as scouted, but nothing else around it developed enough to hold a rotation spot.

name: Tyler Ennis
notes: Syracuse's freshman floor general who opened 25-0 as the starting point guard, praised for court vision, poise and pick-and-roll command beyond his years, but flagged for a small frame, mediocre efficiency (41% FG, 35% from three) and unproven man-to-man defense given Syracuse's zone system. Phoenix took him 18th. Those flags proved prophetic — Ennis never developed into more than emergency depth across four teams (Suns, Bucks, Rockets, Lakers), averaging 4.2/1.9 before his NBA career ended in 2018. Bust: the polish was real, but neither the frame nor the efficiency held up against NBA competition.

name: Gary Harris
notes: Michigan State sophomore shooting guard, a strong shooting-defense-IQ combo (16.7 ppg, plus steal rate) whose ceiling was capped by an ordinary first step and only 35.2% three-point shooting on real volume. Chicago took him 19th and immediately dealt him to Denver. Harris became exactly that translatable 3-and-D two-guard at the NBA level — years as a plus perimeter defender and reliable shooter in Denver's rotation, later continuing that role with Orlando, Milwaukee and Detroit. Solid outcome: never a star, but the precise glue-guy shooting guard scouted, sustained across a long career.

name: Bruno Caboclo
notes: An 18-year-old Brazilian forward almost nobody had scouted in person, famous for Fran Fraschilla's live on-air line that he was "two years away from being two years away" — genuine physical upside (6'9" with real open-floor agility) but zero polish and a total unknown as an NBA prospect. Toronto took him 20th anyway, off Basketball Without Borders buzz. The unknowns never resolved in his favor: Caboclo bounced between the Raptors, Kings, Grizzlies and Rockets without ever carving out a real rotation role, out of the NBA well before his ceiling was ever tested. Bust: the mystery-box pick stayed a mystery box.

name: Semaj Christon
notes: Xavier point guard who entered the draft with an appealing physical/skill combo — good size, speed, and court vision that drew Devin Harris comps — but scouts zeroed in on a real red flag: he made just 7 of 28 three-point attempts in his final college season, a fatal efficiency mark for a lead guard with no other standout offensive tool. That flaw proved decisive. Drafted 55th by Miami and immediately dealt to Oklahoma City, Christon got one real look (2016-17: 64 G, 2.9/2.0/1.4) as an emergency backup point guard before being out of the league by 2017. Textbook bust — the exact weakness identified pre-draft is the reason the career never got off the ground.
